title: Pride, Flattery, and Trickery
objectives: I can use ten words to describe pride, flattery, and trickery.
I can tell how boast, flatter, and gloat are different.
I can find clues in a story that show a character is vain, gullible, or a hypocrite.
I can write a short story or scene using words from this unit.
rationale: Fables, satire, and history are full of characters who brag, flatter, scheme, or are fooled, and fifth graders need exact words to say how those characters behave and why it matters. This unit builds on the connotation work in unit 1 (frugal and stingy): each word carries strong negative attitude, and the differences matter. Boast is about yourself; flatter is about someone else; gloat is about another's failure. Vain, conceited, and gullible describe people, while scheme, deceive, hypocrite, and mock describe what they do or are. The passage is an original animal fable so students can judge character traits from actions and see how vanity and flattery work together. It also gives students language for media literacy: how an advertisement or a stranger may flatter in order to deceive.

words.def: Too quick to believe things, so easy to trick.
words.ex: The gullible shopper believed the ad that said the shoes would make her run twice as fast.
words.ex2: Because Leo was gullible, his cousin convinced him that the moon was made of cheese.
words.nonExample: A person who checks every fact before believing it is not gullible.

apps.academic: A gullible reader may believe false claims online without checking them.
apps.spoken: Don't be gullible; ask who is giving the information.
apps.writing: Use gullible for a person who believes too easily, not for someone who simply trusts a friend.

words.def: Too proud of your looks or abilities.
words.ex: The vain prince stopped in front of every mirror in the castle.
words.ex2: Don't be so vain about your handwriting; it still needs work.
words.nonExample: A person who says thank you to a compliment and moves on is not vain.

apps.academic: In many fables, a vain character is punished for admiring itself too much.
apps.writing: Use vain for someone whose pride is too much, not for ordinary self-respect.

misuse.s: The vain actor never looked in a mirror and never cared how he looked.
misuse.why: A vain person is too proud of his looks and loves mirrors.

visual.alt: A smirking face in front of a mirror.

words.def: Having too high an opinion of yourself.
words.ex: The conceited runner said he would win the race without even training.
words.ex2: Nobody liked the conceited captain who took credit for every goal.
words.nonExample: A player who praises the whole team is not conceited.

segs.m: too high an opinion of oneself

apps.academic: In literature, a conceited character often learns a hard lesson.
apps.spoken: He's so conceited that he forgot to thank the helpers.
apps.writing: Use conceited for someone whose pride shows in how they treat others.

cloze.s: The ___ chef refused to taste anyone else's soup because he was sure his was the best.

cloze2.s: Too ___ to listen to the coach, she kept making the same mistake all season.

misuse.s: The conceited leader thanked everyone on the team and gave all the credit away.
misuse.why: A conceited person takes the credit and thinks too highly of himself; giving credit away is the opposite.

visual.alt: A cool face wearing a crown.

words.def: To talk with too much pride about what you have or do.
words.ex: Marcus liked to boast about his new bike to everyone on the bus.
words.ex2: The cook did not boast; she simply let people taste the stew.
words.nonExample: Quietly thanking the team after a win is not to boast.

apps.academic: In an essay, avoid the urge to boast; give evidence of your success instead.
apps.writing: Use boast when someone talks about what he has or can do in a bragging way.

cloze.s: The knight began to ___ that he had never lost a single jousting match.

cloze2.s: Even though she had won the prize, Amara did not ___ about it; she simply smiled and thanked her teacher.

misuse.s: Humble people love to boast about all the things they have done.
misuse.why: To boast is to brag; humble people do not brag.

visual.alt: A megaphone shouting beside a trophy.

words.frame: I would boast about ___ if I were ___.

words.def: To praise someone too much, or not honestly, to win favor.
words.ex: The cousin tried to flatter his aunt by saying her cooking beat any restaurant's.
words.ex2: Don't flatter me; just tell me what you really think of the plan.
words.nonExample: Telling a friend that her drawing is truly good is not to flatter.

apps.academic: In history, courtiers who flatter a king may keep him from hearing the truth.
apps.spoken: He flatters his teacher so that she gives him extra time.
apps.writing: Use flatter when the praise is too much or has a hidden reason.

cloze.s: The salesman began to ___ the shopper, saying she had the best taste in the whole town.

cloze2.s: Rather than ___ the boss to get a raise, Carlos showed her a list of his accomplishments.

misuse.s: I will flatter you by telling you the honest truth, even though you won't like it.
misuse.why: To flatter is to praise too much or falsely; telling the honest truth is not flattery.

words.def: To enjoy another's failure or your own success in a mean way.
words.ex: Ravi did not gloat when his rival dropped the ball in the final game.
words.ex2: She wanted to gloat about winning, but she remembered how losing feels.
words.nonExample: Quietly smiling at your own good score is not the same as gloating.

apps.academic: In sports writing, a player who gloats after a win is often criticized.
apps.spoken: Please don't gloat about the score.
apps.writing: Use gloat for pleasure that is shown in a way that hurts someone else.

cloze.s: After beating her brother at chess, she could not help but ___ over the win and tease him about it.

cloze2.s: The team did not ___ after the big win; they shook hands with the other players and left.

misuse.s: Kind winners always gloat over the losers and tease them.
misuse.why: Gloating is an unkind way of enjoying a win, so kind winners do not gloat.

visual.alt: A smirking face next to a medal.

words.frame: It is unkind to gloat when ___.

words.def: A secret plan, often a sly or dishonest one.
words.ex: The villain's scheme was to switch the signs and send the travelers the wrong way.
words.ex2: Their scheme to skip the quiz failed when the teacher walked in early.
words.nonExample: A posted schedule that everyone can read is not a scheme.

apps.academic: In mysteries, a detective uncovers the scheme behind the crime.
apps.spoken: Their scheme to get out of homework didn't work.
apps.writing: Use scheme for a secret plan; add details so the reader sees how it works.

cloze.s: The twins' ___ was to hide the clock so that the school day would start late.

cloze2.s: The detective discovered the ___ behind the missing paintings and arrested the thief.

misuse.s: The class posted its scheme on the wall so that everyone could see the open plan.
misuse.why: A scheme is a secret plan, often sly; a plan posted for all to see is not secret.

visual.alt: A detective looking at a secret plan on paper.

words.def: To make fun of someone by copying or teasing them.
words.ex: Some students would mock the new boy's mistake until the teacher stopped them.
words.ex2: It is unkind to mock a person for a mistake.
words.nonExample: Cheering a friend on to try again is not to mock.

apps.academic: Authors sometimes show how a character who mocks others is really afraid.
apps.writing: Use mock for teasing that hurts; it is stronger than joking.

cloze.s: The older kids began to ___ the little boy's high voice, and he ran away in tears.

cloze2.s: Instead of choosing to ___ her mistake, the class offered to help her fix it.

misuse.s: We mock our friends by cheering them on warmly and helping them win.
misuse.why: To mock is to make fun of someone unkindly; cheering them on is not mocking.

visual.alt: A face rolling its eyes in front of a speech bubble.

words.frame: It is unkind to mock someone who ___.

words.def: A person who says one thing but does the opposite.
words.ex: He was a hypocrite, for he told us to recycle and then threw his bottle in the trash.
words.ex2: Don't be a hypocrite: you cannot ask others to be on time if you are always late.
words.nonExample: A person who does what she says is not a hypocrite.
words.rel: saying one thing and doing another

apps.academic: A writer may expose a hypocrite by showing words that do not match actions.
apps.spoken: Don't call me a hypocrite; I changed my mind.
apps.writing: Use hypocrite for someone whose words and actions clearly disagree.

cloze.s: The mayor was a ___: she gave speeches about saving water and then watered her own lawn all day.

cloze2.s: Because he told others to be honest but cheated on every test, the students called him a ___.

misuse.s: She is a hypocrite because she always keeps her word and does what she says.
misuse.why: A hypocrite says one thing and does another; keeping her word is the opposite.

visual.alt: A pair of theater masks, one smiling and one frowning.

words.def: To make someone believe something that is not true.
words.ex: The magician used quick hands to deceive the audience.
words.ex2: She did not mean to deceive her friend, but she left out part of the story.
words.nonExample: Telling a friend the plain truth is not to deceive.

apps.academic: Advertisements that deceive buyers can break the law.
apps.spoken: He tried to deceive me with a fake smile.
apps.writing: Use deceive for causing someone to believe something false, even without spoken lies.

cloze.s: The thief wore a uniform to ___ the guards into letting him walk through the gate.

cloze2.s: Camouflage lets the moth ___ hungry birds, who cannot see it against the tree bark.

misuse.s: The honest guide worked hard to deceive us by telling us only true things.
misuse.why: To deceive is to cause a false belief; telling only the truth is the opposite.

words.frame: Someone might deceive a person by ___.

passage.title: The Magpie and the Mirror Pond
paras: Pia the magpie was vain. Each morning she stood at the edge of Mirror Pond, admiring her blue-black feathers. She was so conceited that she believed no bird in the forest could match her, and she loved to boast about her collection of buttons, coins, and glass beads. "I have the finest treasures in the valley," she told every bird who passed.

A raccoon named Rook listened with a sly smile. He meant to deceive her, and he had a scheme. "Pia, your feathers shine like midnight," he began to flatter. "A bird so wise should lead the forest council." Pia was gullible, and she believed every word. "The council meets on the far shore," Rook said, "and you must bring your finest treasures to prove your worth."

Pia was halfway across the pond with her sack when the jay Juno called out. Juno had mocked Pia for weeks, yet she was a hypocrite, because she bragged about her own singing every evening. This time, though, she spoke the truth: Rook had slipped into the nest to steal the rest of the collection. Pia raced home.

Rook fled with a single button. Juno did not gloat, though she could have. "Next time," she said, "ask why someone praises you so much." Pia nodded and, for the first time, said nothing about her feathers.

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "gullible" most nearly means
choices: very proud of one's own looks
easily tricked because one believes too quickly
qs.why: Pia believes every word Rook says without questioning it, so gullible means easy to fool.

choices: to take Pia's place on the forest council
to teach Pia to share her treasures
to get Pia away from her nest so he could steal her collection
to win a race across the pond
qs.why: Rook flattered Pia into taking her best treasures across the pond so he could slip into her nest and steal the rest.

qs.q: Why does the author call Juno a hypocrite?
choices: She mocked Pia for bragging but bragged about her own singing.
She did not warn Pia in time.
She was jealous of Pia's collection.
qs.why: Juno made fun of Pia for bragging while she herself bragged about her singing, which is saying one thing and doing another.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Juno did not gloat?
choices: She called out to Pia across the pond.
She said she could have said more but chose to give advice.
qs.why: The text says Juno did not gloat, though she could have, and instead offered a lesson about praise.

qs.q: Which lesson does the story teach?
choices: Anyone who loves praise too much can be fooled by flattery.
qs.why: Pia's vanity makes her easy to flatter, and the flattery leads to the trick, so the lesson is about being fooled through praise.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten words for the way people act when they are proud, flattering, or tricky. The passage is an original animal fable in which vanity and flattery lead to a scheme. The unit builds careful, precise language for character traits and gives students vocabulary for evaluating persuasion and media.

notes.va.gullible.adj: Gullible describes a person who is too trusting, not stupid. Frame it as a trait that anyone can show in a given moment. Ask students for ways to protect against being tricked, such as asking questions and checking facts.
notes.va.vain.adj: Vain here means too proud of looks or abilities. The word also has an older sense, in vain, meaning without success. Teach the first and mention that the two senses are related: both carry the idea of emptiness.
notes.va.conceited.adj: Conceited and vain overlap. Vain is often about looks; conceited is about an inflated opinion of oneself in general. Have students place both on the how much you think of yourself ladder.
notes.va.boast.v: Boast is to talk with too much pride about yourself. Contrast with brag, which is the same, and with feel proud, which is a feeling and not a bad one. Students may think any positive statement about oneself is boasting; clarify that it is the too much pride that makes it boasting.
notes.va.flatter.v: Flatter is praise that is too much or not sincere, given to win something. Students often think flattery is simply a compliment. Contrast: a compliment is honest, flattery has a motive. Use the Rook example.
notes.va.gloat.v: Gloat means to enjoy another's failure or your own win in an unkind way. The feeling is not the problem; showing it in a way that hurts someone is. Have students act out gloating versus quietly celebrating.
notes.va.scheme.n: Scheme can be a noun or a verb. The noun, taught here, is a secret plan, often sly or dishonest. Students may also know a neutral sense, a plan or system, as in a color scheme; mention it and keep the taught sense.
notes.va.mock.v: Mock is to make fun of someone, often by copying them. Note that mock also has other senses, such as a mock test, which means practice. Keep the taught sense and warn students to check context.
notes.va.hypocrite.n: A hypocrite says one thing and does another, such as someone who tells others not to litter and then drops trash. Ask students to find a hypocrite in the passage and show the two sides of the character's behavior.
notes.va.deceive.v: Deceive is to make someone believe something that is not true. Contrast with lie: a lie is words, but deceiving can be done by actions. The noun is deceit. Ask students how Rook deceived Pia, using words and actions.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The author says Rook began to flatter Pia. The words shine like midnight and wise enough to lead the council are praise, but Rook wants her treasures, not her happiness. So this is not honest praise. This is flattery, because the praise has a hidden motive.'
discuss: Which of the ten words describes a person you would not want as a friend, and why?
Which word describes a behavior that is easy to fix, and which describes a harder habit?
misconceptions: Flattery is the same as a kind compliment.
Vain and conceited mean exactly the same thing.
A gullible person is silly or not smart.
Gloat means to feel happy for any reason.
A hypocrite is a liar; a hypocrite acts against what he says.

Write a fable of your own with a flatterer and a gullible character, and add a moral.

Return to the ten words after two days, again at one week, in character descriptions.
